claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed, intact native oxide layer.
The native oxide layer on Q235 steel acts as a protective barrier at room temperature.
An intact native oxide suppresses corrosion by limiting ingress of corrosive ions.
Elevated temperature generates thermal stress in the native oxide layer on Q235 steel.
Thermal stress causes microcracking or increased porosity in the native oxide layer.
Microcracking or porosity exposes the underlying steel to chloride ions.
Exposure of the underlying steel through oxide defects accelerates localized corrosion.
Q235 specimens exposed to 3.5 wt.% NaCl at approximately 100°C will have greater mass loss than untreated specimens exposed at approximately 25°C.
Q235 specimens exposed at elevated temperature will have greater pitting density than the room-temperature reference.
Q235 specimens exposed at elevated temperature will have lower electrochemical impedance than the room-temperature reference.
Pre-etching the native oxide will increase corrosion indicators relative to the untreated reference.
The relevant structural mediator is native-oxide thickness, continuity, and defect density.
The proposed mechanism applies under static, chloride-rich conditions with controlled pH and temperature.
Changes in alloy composition, surface finish, or flow conditions may alter the proposed mechanism.
A controlled comparison should hold chloride concentration, pH, exposure duration, surface finish, starting oxide thickness, and flow conditions constant while varying temperature.
Failure to observe both increased corrosion indicators and oxide degradation at elevated temperature would falsify the proposed thermal-oxide-deterioration mechanism.
